title: Bakhshali manuscript
summary: The Bakhshali manuscript is a mathematical text on 70 birch-bark leaves, found by a farmer in 1881 at Bakhshali near Peshawar, in present-day Pakistan. Radiocarbon tests by Oxford in 2017 dated its leaves from 224-383 CE to 885-993 CE, nearly 500 years apart. It contains dots used as zero placeholders, older than the symbols scholars had earlier accepted.

uncertainty.note: Range spans the earliest and latest folio ranges tested: folio 16 at 224-383 CE and folio 33 at 885-993 CE; folio 17 gave 680-779 CE. Scholars earlier placed the text in the 8th-12th centuries.

where.historical_name: Bakhshali, a farm village near Peshawar, in the northwest of British India (found 1881)

importance.justification: Its radiocarbon dates push the use of a dot for zero in India back centuries.

sources.title: Illuminating India: starring the oldest recorded origins of zero, the Bakhshali manuscript
sources.author: Science Museum Group

sources.title: Carbon Dating Reveals the History of Zero Is Older Than Previously Thought

reviewer_note: Least sure of the single date: the leaves differ by about 500 years, and the Smithsonian article reports only the earliest range. The pin is the Wikidata point for Bakhshali village in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; the pages say only "near Peshawar", so uncertainty is wide. Scholarly dispute of the Oxford dating was not read on an opened page and is not claimed.
